passage:
I was in the passenger seat, so I saw all of it. My friend Irawati got her licence in March and drives more carefully than anyone I know; she even slows down for speed breakers that aren't there.
That evening her manager called about the next day's shift, and she took the call on speaker. We came up to the zebra crossing by the vegetable market. An old man with a cloth bag was already halfway across, in a white kurta, right under a streetlight. Irawati didn't slow. I shouted her name, and she stamped on the brake. The man stopped, stared at us, and walked on.
She sat gripping the wheel and whispered, "He was right in front of me."
I can't say exactly what went on in her head. I do know that the next morning she put her phone in the glovebox before starting the car.
Sarika

qa.q: Where was the old man when Irawati didn't slow down?
qa.a: He was already halfway across the zebra crossing by the vegetable market, right under a streetlight.

qa.q: What does Irawati's whisper, "He was right in front of me," suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She seems shocked and shaken that she missed someone in plain view; the call had taken her attention even though her eyes were on the road.

qa.q: What choice did Irawati make the next morning, and why is it a good guard?
qa.a: She put the phone in the glovebox before starting; a fixed habit works better than trusting herself to stay careful during a call.

qa.q: How does Sarika see Irawati after the near miss?
qa.a: Sarika still sees her as an unusually careful driver and does not claim to know her thoughts, which suggests the slip was about attention, not bad character.

grounding: It shows a careful young driver on a phone call who misses a pedestrian in plain view and then builds a habit to guard against it.

passage:
Monday: Tenzin, nineteen, drives the family van to college and follows the map on the dashboard phone, tapping in new stops while moving. "I'm a good driver," Tenzin tells Binita, who rides along. "I can manage."
Wednesday: Near the primary school gate, Tenzin looks down to change the route. A girl in a blue uniform steps onto the crossing with her hand raised. Binita yells. The van stops a metre short. The girl's mother pulls her back, and Tenzin can't stop apologising. "She was right there. How did I not see her?"
Saturday: Tenzin sits in the parked van and sets the whole route before turning the key. The phone goes face down in the side pocket. "New rule," Tenzin tells Binita. "If the plan changes, you read it out, or I pull over."

qa.q: Where did the girl in the blue uniform step onto the crossing?
qa.a: She stepped onto the crossing near the primary school gate.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin feel confident on Monday about tapping in stops while driving?
qa.a: Tenzin believed a good driver could manage both, so glancing down for a second felt safe; Wednesday showed attention has limits whatever the skill.

qa.q: What changed on Saturday, and why is it a better guard than trying harder?
qa.a: Tenzin set the route before starting, put the phone face down and made a rule to pull over or let Binita read, so there is no reason to look down while driving.

qa.q: What might the girl's mother have felt on Wednesday?
qa.a: She was probably terrified for a moment, pulling her daughter back from a van whose driver seemed to be looking somewhere else. 😰

grounding: It shows a young driver using a map app who misses a child on a crossing and then sets rules that remove the distraction.

passage:
Akash, sit down before you take the car keys. Your Aparna Masi wants to tell you about the year she turned twenty-one.
I had a small scooter and a new job at the bank. One evening my friend rang, and I tucked the phone inside my helmet so I could talk while riding. I thought I was being clever. At the bus stand, a woman with a baby stepped off the kerb, right under the tube light, in a bright red sari. I did not see her. I mean it, beta. My eyes were on the road, and I did not see her. The conductor shouted, I braked, and my front wheel stopped by her feet.
I was not a careless girl. I was a girl on a phone call. That is why I switch mine off before I ride, even today, and why you will too.

qa.q: What was the woman at the bus stand wearing?
qa.a: She was wearing a bright red sari and carrying a baby, right under the tube light.

qa.q: Why did Aparna think tucking the phone into the helmet was clever?
qa.a: Aparna felt confident and clever, believing that as long as her eyes were on the road, talking cost nothing; the near miss showed her attention had gone to the call.

qa.q: What habit did Aparna build after that evening?
qa.a: She switches her phone off before riding, a fixed habit that guards against a limit that good intentions alone cannot.

qa.q: Why might Akash take this more seriously because it comes from Aparna herself?
qa.a: Hearing a careful elder admit she nearly hit someone shows Akash it can happen to anyone, not just careless drivers, so the rule feels fair rather than insulting.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, as a young rider on a call, she missed a pedestrian in plain view and why a habit now guards her.

passage: Rain hammered the windscreen of the delivery pickup, and Bhupen, nineteen, had forty minutes to reach the last three shops in Guwahati before they closed. His sister Sabina sat beside him with the parcels. The phone on the dashboard showed the map, and then his boss's name flashed. Bhupen tapped speaker. "Yes sir, reaching, sir." At the crossing near the school, a man in a grey raincoat stepped onto the road, right in front of the headlights. "BHUPEN!" Sabina screamed. He stamped on the brake. The pickup stopped a hand's width away. The man slapped the bonnet and walked on. Bhupen's hands shook. "I was looking ahead," he whispered. "I swear I didn't see him." That evening he wrote on a card and taped it to the dashboard: Calls only when parked.

qa.q: What was Bhupen doing when he reached the crossing near the school?
qa.a: He was on speaker with his boss, saying, "Yes sir, reaching, sir."

qa.q: Why did Bhupen whisper "I swear I didn't see him"?
qa.a: He was shaken and confused, because his eyes were on the road but his attention was on his boss's call, so the man simply didn't register.

qa.q: What rule did Bhupen make, and why is a rule better than trying harder?
qa.a: Calls only when parked; attention has limits that effort can't fix, so a fixed habit stops the phone from pulling it away.

qa.q: What was that moment like for Sabina?
qa.a: She was terrified, seeing the man before her brother did and screaming just in time, and was probably still shaking afterwards.

grounding: A young driver taking a call in rain and time pressure misses a pedestrian in plain view, then sets a rule to guard his attention.

passage:
Anirban had had his licence for eight months and was proud of never having scraped his father's car. On Saturday evening, driving through Kolkata's Gariahat with his friend Jeevan, he was scrolling the phone in its holder for a song. The signal turned green. A woman with two bags of vegetables was halfway across the zebra crossing, clear as day under the streetlight. Anirban rolled forward. Jeevan yelled, "Stop!" The car jerked. The woman glared through the windscreen. Anirban sat frozen. "She wasn't there," he said.
"She was there the whole time," Jeevan said quietly. "You were picking a song."
At home Anirban switched on the phone's driving mode and made a rule: music chosen before starting, phone out of reach.

qa.q: What was Anirban looking for on his phone?
qa.a: A song.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel after Jeevan yelled "Stop!", and what shows it?
qa.a: Anirban felt shaken and stunned, sitting frozen and insisting "She wasn't there", because his attention had been on picking a song.

qa.q: What habit did Anirban set up, and why could it work?
qa.a: Choosing music before starting and keeping the phone out of reach, so nothing pulls his attention off the road while driving.

qa.q: How might the woman on the crossing have felt as the car rolled toward her?
qa.a: She was likely frightened and angry, having crossed properly under a streetlight only to have a car move toward her.

grounding: A careful young driver picking a song misses a pedestrian in plain view, showing a limit of attention that habit must guard.

passage: Dilnaz, you asked why I keep my phone in the glovebox now. Here's why. I'm Deepika. Three months ago I was driving Papa's car to college, talking to the internship coordinator on speaker and checking the map at the same time. The road was clear, I thought. At a zebra crossing near the market, an old woman with a shopping bag was already halfway across. In plain view. I saw her only when she was right in front of the bonnet. I stamped on the brake. The car stopped a hand's width from her. She wasn't hurt, just shaking, and so was I. I got out, apologised, and walked her to the other side. I'm not a careless person. But my attention was on that call. So now it's a rule, not a choice: glovebox, silent, before the engine starts.

qa.q: Where does Deepika keep the phone now?
qa.a: In the glovebox.

qa.q: Why does Deepika say 'I'm not a careless person'?
qa.a: Deepika feels shaken and ashamed, and wants to explain that the near miss came from attention being on the call, not from not caring.

qa.q: Why is a fixed rule better than trying to be more careful each time?
qa.a: Attention has limits, so a habit like phone in the glovebox on silent before starting guards against distraction without relying on willpower.

qa.q: What was the moment like for the old woman at the crossing?
qa.a: She was frightened and shaking, suddenly facing a car that stopped just a hand's width from her.

grounding: Shows a young driver on a call missing a pedestrian in plain view and adopting a firm rule against phone use while driving.

passage:
Monday. Sumit rode his scooter to his part-time job with one earphone in, taking calls from his manager at every signal. It felt efficient.
Wednesday. Near the school on Station Road, he was on a call about a delivery when a boy in a blue uniform stepped off the kerb. Sumit hadn't seen him at all, though the boy had been standing there in plain sight. He braked hard; the scooter skidded and stopped just short. The boy's mother pulled him back, shouting. Sumit's hands shook for an hour.
The following Monday. Sumit told his sister Rajni he had set his phone to reply 'Riding, will call back' automatically. He left the earphones at home. "I thought I could do both," he said. "I can't. Nobody can."

qa.q: What colour was the boy's uniform?
qa.a: Blue.

qa.q: How did Sumit feel after braking near the school?
qa.a: Sumit felt shaken and frightened, his hands shaking for an hour, realising he hadn't seen a boy standing in plain sight.

qa.q: What rule did Sumit set, and why is it wise?
qa.a: An automatic 'Riding, will call back' reply and no earphones, so calls can't pull his attention while riding.

qa.q: How might the boy's mother have felt as she pulled him back?
qa.a: She was probably terrified and angry, shouting at the rider who hadn't seen her son.

grounding: Shows a young rider on a call failing to see a child in plain view, and building a habit to guard against it.

passage: Ritu, before you start the car with that phone on your lap, let your Rashmi bua tell you something. I was twenty-one, driving my father's old car through Ludhiana, and I had just bought a new cassette. I was pushing it into the player, eyes on the road, I was sure of it, when a cyclist came through the crossing right in front of me. He had been there all along. I simply hadn't seen him. I missed him by a hair, but he fell off in fright and scraped his palms. I stopped, helped him up and paid for his bandages, shaking the whole time. That evening my father didn't shout. He said, "Your eyes were on the road. Your mind was on the tape." From then on, the tape went in before the engine started. Now it's your phone. Glovebox, beta.

qa.q: What was young Rashmi doing when the cyclist came through?
qa.a: She was pushing a new cassette into the player.

qa.q: How did young Rashmi feel after the cyclist fell?
qa.a: Rashmi felt shaken and guilty, shaking the whole time while helping him up, shocked that she hadn't seen him at all.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Bua's story, and what habit came from it?
qa.a: Her father's words that her mind was on the tape; from then on the tape went in before the engine started, and now she tells Ritu to put the phone in the glovebox.

qa.q: What was the moment like for the cyclist?
qa.a: The cyclist got a fright, fell off and scraped his palms, though he was helped up.

grounding: Shows a young driver failing to see a cyclist in plain view while distracted, and turning it into a rule for the next generation.

passage:
Aditi had passed her driving test a month ago. That evening she was driving her aunt Noor's car to the pharmacy in heavy rain, wipers thumping, and her phone buzzed with a call from her project group.

She answered on speaker. "Yes, I'll send the slides tonight..."

At the zebra crossing, a man with a black umbrella was already halfway across. She saw the lights. She saw the road. She didn't see him until Noor shouted, "Stop!"

Aditi slammed the brakes. The man jumped back, shaken, and waved his umbrella at her.

Her hands were trembling on the wheel. She ended the call, pulled over by the pharmacy, and put her phone in the glove box. "I was looking straight ahead," she whispered.

qa.q: Who was crossing at the zebra crossing?
qa.a: A man with a black umbrella was already halfway across.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when she whispered "I was looking straight ahead"?
qa.a: She felt frightened and shaken, and confused that she missed him while her eyes were on the road.

qa.q: What did Aditi do right after the near miss, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She ended the call, pulled over and put her phone in the glove box, so calls can't pull her attention while driving.

qa.q: How might the man with the umbrella have felt?
qa.a: He was probably scared and angry, having nearly been hit while crossing properly.

grounding: A young driver on a call misses a pedestrian in plain view, a limit of attention that habits must guard against.

passage:
Anand had driven the same road in Bengaluru every day for a year, to his job at the bakery supply store. He knew every pothole.

That Tuesday he was checking a delivery route on the map app while waiting at the signal. When it turned green, he glanced up, pressed the accelerator, and looked down again.

A small boy crossing with his father stepped off the kerb. Anand's colleague Asif, in the passenger seat, yelled. Anand braked hard, missing the boy by an arm's length.

The father held the boy tight and stared at him. Anand felt his face burn.

"I'm not a careless person," he told Asif later, still shaking. "I just thought I could look quickly."

That evening he set the route before starting and mounted the phone out of reach.

qa.q: How far was the boy from the car when Anand braked?
qa.a: He missed the boy by an arm's length.

qa.q: Why did Anand tell Asif "I'm not a careless person"?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and shaken, and wanted to explain that he thought a quick look was harmless, not that he didn't care.

qa.q: What changes did Anand make, and why do they help?
qa.a: He set the route before starting and put the phone out of reach, so habit protects his attention instead of willpower.

qa.q: What might the father have felt holding the boy tight?
qa.a: The father was probably terrified and angry, relieved his son was safe.

grounding: A young driver checking an app misses a pedestrian in plain view, a limit of attention that needs habits to guard against.

passage:
"Reena, you just drove past the school crossing without slowing down."

"What? No, I didn't."

"You did. There was a lady with a pram. She had to step back."

"I was just finishing this voice note to Mausi."

Sarita turned in her seat. "You were looking right at the road."

"Exactly! I'd have seen her."

"But you didn't."

Reena went quiet. Her hands tightened on the steering wheel.

"I really didn't see her," she said finally. "That's... horrible."

"It's not that you're a bad driver," Sarita said. "It's that the voice note took your head somewhere else."

Reena pulled into a side lane and stopped. She handed Sarita her phone. "Keep it till we get home."

qa.q: Who had to step back at the school crossing?
qa.a: A lady with a pram.

qa.q: How did Reena feel when she realised she hadn't seen the lady?
qa.a: She felt shocked and horrified, gripping the wheel tighter when she understood what almost happened.

qa.q: What did Reena do next, and why was it a good choice?
qa.a: She pulled over and gave Sarita her phone, removing the distraction for the rest of the drive.

qa.q: How does Sarita see Reena's mistake?
qa.a: Sarita sees it as a limit of attention rather than bad driving, and she stays calm and supportive.

grounding: A young driver sending a voice note misses a pedestrian in plain view; it's a limit of attention, not character.

passage:
Last month I learned something about my own brain that still scares me. I'm Dilnaz, and I'd had my licence for five months.
Anjali and I were driving back from college. My phone rang: my mother, about dinner. I put it on speaker, both hands on the wheel, eyes on the road. I thought I was being responsible.
At the zebra crossing near the vegetable market, a man with a cart was already halfway across. In plain view. I didn't see him. Anjali screamed my name and I braked hard. We stopped with a foot to spare.
My eyes had been on the road the whole time. My attention had been on dinner.
I pulled over, shaking, and told my mother I'd call back. Since then I have one rule: phone on silent in the glovebox before I start the car. Not because I'm careless. Because my attention can only be in one place.

qa.q: How long had Dilnaz had the licence?
qa.a: Dilnaz had had the licence for five months.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel after braking?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt shaken and frightened, realising the eyes had been on the road but attention was on dinner.

qa.q: What rule does Dilnaz follow now, and why?
qa.a: Phone on silent in the glovebox before starting the car, because attention can only be in one place.

qa.q: How might the man with the cart have felt?
qa.a: He was likely startled and frightened, seeing a car brake hard just before reaching him.

grounding: Shows a young driver on a speaker call who misses a pedestrian in plain view, a limit of attention that a firm habit guards against.

passage:
Driving school note, lesson 14. Written by Zeenat, instructor.
Sarika drives well in quiet conditions. Today we practised on the market road. She asked to follow the map on her phone, mounted on the dashboard, "just to learn the route".
At the second crossing, a schoolgirl stepped out in plain view. Sarika was looking at the map and did not react. I used the dual brake. We stopped safely.
Sarika was very upset. "I was looking right there. How did I not see her?" I told her it is not a sign she is a bad person or a bad driver. Attention is limited, and the map was using it.
What I did next: we agreed the phone stays off the dashboard during lessons, and that before she drives alone she will set any route beforehand and use voice directions only. We'll repeat the market road next week.

qa.q: What did Zeenat use to stop the car?
qa.a: Zeenat used the dual brake.

qa.q: Why was Sarika so upset?
qa.a: Sarika felt shocked and ashamed, having looked right at the crossing and still not seen the schoolgirl.

qa.q: What did Zeenat and Sarika agree, and why is it wise?
qa.a: The phone stays off the dashboard during lessons, and routes are set beforehand with voice directions, so attention stays on the road.

qa.q: How might the schoolgirl have experienced the moment?
qa.a: The schoolgirl was probably startled to see a car stop suddenly beside her.

grounding: Shows, in an instructor's note, a young driver who misses a pedestrian in plain view while following a phone map, and the rules set to guard against it.

passage:
Sunday night.
Scary thing today. I was driving Aditi back from the station, and my boss called about Monday's shift. I answered. Just a short call, I told myself.
At the roundabout a boy on a cycle came from the left. He was right there, in plain view, in a bright red shirt. I didn't see him until Aditi shouted. I braked, he wobbled, nobody was hurt. He glared at me, and he was right to.
I keep thinking: I'm not a careless person. I was looking. But my attention was on my boss's voice, not the road.
Aditi said, "You don't need to feel like a villain. You need a rule." So here's the rule, written down so I remember: phone in the boot on every drive. If someone calls, they can wait twenty minutes.
Kishore

qa.q: What colour was the boy's shirt?
qa.a: The boy's shirt was bright red.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel after the near-miss?
qa.a: Kishore felt shaken and guilty, knowing there had been looking but no real attention on the road.

qa.q: What rule did Kishore write down, and why does it help?
qa.a: Phone in the boot on every drive, so calls can't pull attention from the road.

qa.q: How might the boy on the cycle have felt?
qa.a: The boy was likely frightened and angry, which is why he glared.

grounding: Shows a young driver on a call who misses a cyclist in plain view, and sets a rule to guard against the limits of attention.
